## The LASSO

[Last time](./notes09.qmd), we argued that we could use the "zero-norm": 

$$\|\bx\|_0 = \text{Number of Non-Zero Elements of } \bx$$

to characterize _sparse_ models. Specifically, recall that the $\|\cdot\|_0$
norm works like: 

$$\begin{align*}
\|(1, 2, 3)\|_0 &= 3  \\
\|(0, 0, 0)\|_0 &= 0 \\
\|(0, 2, 0)\|_0 = 1
\end{align*}$$

Like the sum-of-squares norm that we used for ridge regression, this captures
a notion of 'not too big'-ness (and makes a bias-variance gambit), but instead
of judging a model by _how big_ its coefficients are, it judges it by _how many_
coefficients it uses. We saw that ridge regression had the ability to 
'automatically' make our model coefficients smaller and only make them big
when the data demanded it (at a price of $\lambda$); use of the $\ell_0$-norm
will do the same thing. 

In our constrained form, this looks like: 

$$\argmin_{\substack{\bbeta \in \R^p \\ \|\bbeta\|_0 \leq k}} \text{TrainingMSE}(\bbeta).$$
Here, we're saying find me the best linear model **using no more than $k$
of the total $p$ features** as measured by training MSE. As with ridge 
regression, this is a _hard constraint_ and will never select more than $k$
features.[^k_features] We can translate this to 'penalty' form: 

$$\argmin_{\bbeta \in \R^p} \text{TrainingMSE}(\bbeta) + \lambda \|\bbeta\|_0.$$

Here, we will include a feature if and only if it reduces our Training MSE by
$\lambda$ or more over the next best alternative. (Can you argue why?)

Many of the _model selection_ tools you have seen in previous courses are 
instances of this set-up, which is generally called 'best subsets' because we
seek the best subset of $k$ predictors (again, as measured by Training MSE). 
Things like _forward stepwise_ or _backward stepwise_ model selection are
algorithms that attempt to solve the above problems, typically based on some
theoretically driven ($p$-value, $F$-test, ANOVA, *etc*) choice of $\lambda$. 

This is all well and good for simple problems, where brute force can be 
sufficient. With $p$ possible features, an exhaustive search requires us to 
solve $2^p$ different OLS problems. At the scale of $p\approx 10-20$, this may
not be completely unrealistic for small data sets where the individual OLS fits
are near instant. (Applying OLS to the penguins data $2^20$ times takes a bit 
under 8 minutes on my laptop.) But as problems get bigger and bigger, this
quickly becomes essentially impossible. 

First order (gradient) methods don't really help here, because the gradient
of $\|\cdot\|_0$ gives us no information. (Recall that it is flat everywhere
except $0$ where it jumps down by 1 at a single point.) So it is hard to beat
the 'wander around randomly trying things' strategy in a systematic fashion. 

This leaves us with a set of alternatives: we can either

- Solve the _exact_ best-subsets problem _approximately_; or
- Solve an _approximation_ to best-subsets _exactly_. 

(I suppose we could also solve the approximation approximately, but we don't
typically need to go quite that far.) As mentioned above, you already know some
approaches for _approximate_ solves for the _exact_ problem, so now let's look
instead at how we might _approximate_ the best-subsets problem. 

In approximating the best subsets problem, what are we looking for? We want to
find another similar problem that is: 

- Easy to solve with first order methods
- Has a solution that is 'close' to the best-subsets problem
- Inherits the desirable properties of best subsets (automatic model selection)

Ridge regression actually gets us surprisingly close: it's certainly easy to 
solve and typically gives us a solution with many small values. It's not 
unreasonable to think that we could just 'throw away' the small values, keeping
the larger ones. This -- "thresholded ridge" -- is a viable strategy more often
than textbooks might suggest, but it still has some problems: 

- We now have two knobs (how much ridge + how small is small enough to 
  safely discard) to tune
- Ridge typically pushes many features down to zero at the same rate

Because ridge cares much more about the difference between 10 and 11 
($11^2 - 10^2 = 21$) than 2 and 1 ($2^2 - 1^2 = 3$), ridge regression will put
the bulk of its shrinkage activity on the biggest coefficients, leaving the
'reasonably small' things alone until $\lambda$ is quite large. This is exactly
the opposite of what we want. We'd much prefer a model that puts its shrinkage
into the small coefficients, leaving the larger values unscathed. 

Sadly, this is not quite doable, but we can at least find a closely related 
problem that shrinks everything, high and low, _at the same rate_. Our hope
here, is that a large value, say 11, is shrunk to 10, but a small value, say 1, 
gets pushed all the way to 0. In essence, we want a 'bigness' measure that
is essentially _linear_ in the inputs. 

And we have one! Remember back a few lectures when we talked about different
vector 'norms' - measures of bigness or size. At the time, we looked at our
'Euclidean' ($\ell_2$)

$$\|\bx\|_2^2 = \sum_i x_i^2$$

distance because it was geometrically familiar and 'played nice' with
the squares of least squares, but we also had our _taxicab_ 
(Manhattan or $\ell_1$) norm: 

$$\|\bx\|_1 = \sqrt[1]{\sum_i |x_i|^1} = \sum_i |x_i|$$

That is, the sum of the absolute values of $\bx$. If we plot the absolute
value function, we see that it has exactly that linear type of behavior we wanted: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
data.frame(x=seq(-2, 2, length.out=401)) |>
    mutate(y=abs(x)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab(expression(x)) + 
    ylab(expression(abs(x))) + 
    ggtitle("Absolute Value Function / One Coordinate of the Taxicab Norm")
```

If we use something like this as a penalty, it should stand a much better chance
at 'zeroing' out coefficients (like $\ell_0$) while still being something we
can actually solve efficiently (like $\ell_2$ / ridge).[^incremental]

[^k_features]: And because more features essentially always helps, this will
essentially always select exactly $k$ features. 

[^incremental]: A bit more technical, but it's worth thinking about what happens
to a value of $\beta$ that the data suggests is small; the OLS squared term 
will have a gradient proportional to $\beta$ (derivative of squared term is linear)
while the derivative of the absolute value will always be $\pm 1$ (whichever
pushes towards the zero point). Hence, the absolute value will push 'harder' than
the MSE term, giving us exact zeros. Contrast this to ridge, where we have have
two terms both with a linear gradient; one (data/MSE) pushes us away from zero,
while the other (ridge penalty) pushes us towards zero and we have no reason to
think we'll land exactly on zero. 

And, _mirabile dictu_, this heuristic argument not only works, but works well
and gives us a problem that we can solve efficiently. I present you with the
`LASSO`: 

$$\argmin_{\bbeta} \text{TrainingMSE}(\bbeta) + \lambda \|\bbeta\|_1 = \argmin_{\bbeta} \text{TrainingMSE}(\bbeta) + \lambda \sum_{i=1}^p |\beta_i|$$

For $\lambda \to 0$, like ridge, we get back to OLS, but as $\lambda$ gets large
we'll actually get _exact_ zeros out. (This is actually the 'easy to solve' 
problem that is closest to best squares and so we call it the 
'tightest relaxation'.) It lives on the magic margin of 'easy to solve' while
also 'giving exact zeros', a territory occupied by nothing else. 

So what is `LASSO`? Well, it is firstly a somewhat janky acronym for the 
_Least Absolute Selection and Shrinkage Operator_: 

- _Least_. We will apply this as a 'bolt-on' to our general minimum training
  error / ERM paradigm. 
- _Absolute_. We penalize according to absolute values, not squares. 
- _Selection_. This will automatically select certain coefficients and zero
  out others
- _Shrinkage_. While this will only push some features _all the way_ to zero, 
  it will push the rest _towards_ zero, doing a bit of a bias-variance gambit
  on all features, even the ones it keeps. 
- _Operator_. Generic math word to make the acronym work. 

While on the nice end of the math spectrum, this is still not quite as simple
as OLS and ridge regression, so we do need to use an iterative algorithm to
find the solution. The `glmnet` package that we used for ridge regression can
also solve LASSO problems and, indeed, was originally developed for LASSO-type
problems. 

We start with the same data as before: 

```{r winesetup}
#| cache: true
# Generated with help of Gemini
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(tidyr)
library(glmnet)

# 1. Ingest static TidyTuesday snapshot
raw_wine <- read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2019/2019-05-28/winemag-data-130k-v2.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
)

# 2. Subsample to create a controlled p > n setting (n = 100)
set.seed(3106)
wine_sample <- raw_wine |>
    filter(variety == "Pinot Noir", !is.na(points), !is.na(description)) |>
    slice_sample(n = 100) |>
    mutate(wine_id = row_number()) |>
    select(wine_id, points, description)

# 3. Tokenize, strip stopwords/digits, and prune singletons
tidy_words <- wine_sample |>
    unnest_tokens(word, description) |>
    anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
    filter(!str_detect(word, "^[0-9]+$"))

frequent_words <- tidy_words |>
    distinct(wine_id, word) |>
    count(word) |>
    filter(n >= 2)

# 4. Reshape to wide DTM via pivot_wider()
dtm <- tidy_words |>
    semi_join(frequent_words, by = "word") |>
    count(wine_id, word) |>
    pivot_wider(
        names_from = word,
        values_from = n,
        values_fill = 0
    )

# 5. Build design matrix X and continuous target y
aligned <- wine_sample |>
    select(wine_id, points) |>
    inner_join(dtm, by = "wine_id")

X <- aligned |> select(-wine_id, -points) |> as.matrix()
y <- aligned$points
```

Next, we apply `glmnet`, but here we set `alpha=1` (or just leave it 
unspecified since $\alpha=1$ is the default) to fit the LASSO: 

```{r}
library(glmnet)
library(broom)
glmnet(X, y, lambda=1) |> tidy()
```

From here, we see that at $\lambda=1$, only three features (three words) are 
selected and to a non-oeniphile, they seem pretty reasonable to me. 

As with ridge regression, getting the _right_ value of $\lambda$ is a tricky
problem. Before we do this, let's note that `glmnet` provides several nice
"multi-$\lambda$" features. In particular, `glmnet` will

1) Automatically find the value of $\lambda$ that makes all your coefficients 
   zero and stop there (so-called $\lambda_{\max}$)
2) Solve for a wide range of $\lambda$ ending at $\lambda_{\max}$
3) Do so in a clever way that makes solving at 100 different $\lambda$'s almost
   as fast as solving at a single $\lambda$: 
   
```{r}
glmnet(X, y) |> plot()
```

This looks similar to the _regularization paths_ we saw for ride regression, but
with some interesting differences: 

1) The paths are a bit 'pointier': while the ridge paths were smooth, here we
   see some artifacts of the 'sharp corner' in the absolute value penalty
2) The paths eventually hit zero and stop. This is exactly the _shrinkage_ we
   expect! While it is possible for a feature to hit zero for a while and then
   'reactivate' (possibly even with a different sign!), the typical behavior
   is for a feature to be shrunk 'out of existence' permanently. 
3) We can now make some sense of the values along the top. These measure the
   number of _non-zero_ coefficients. At the left side of the plot, where
   $-\log(\lambda)$ is small $\leftrightarrow$ $\lambda$ is large, we see that
   most features are 'zeroed out' and only a few remain. As we move to the right,
   more and more features get 'activated', until we stop at $n=p$ total features.
   (We will _never_ select *more* than $n$ features.)
   
When talking about ridge, we found that the $$\hat{\beta} = \frac_{SS_{XY}}{SS_{XX} + \lambda}$$ 'metaphor' was helpful to demonstrate the form of shrinkage. We can't
get a nice expression like that for LASSO (and remember that was even a bit
informal for ridge) except in one very special case. If 

$$\bX = \begin{pmatrix} 1 &0 & 0  & \dots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \dots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

we have an exact solution: 

$$\hat{\beta}_i = \begin{cases} y_i - \lambda & y_i > \lambda \\ 0 & 0 & |y_i| \leq \lambda \\ y_i + \lambda & y_i < -\lambda \end{cases}$$

It's a bit easier to compare this to the ridge solution 
$\hat{\beta}_i = y_i / (1 + \lambda)$ and the OLS solution $\hat{\beta} = y_i$
visually: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
lambda <- 1
data.frame(y = seq(-3, 3, length.out=601)) |> 
    mutate(beta_ols = y, 
           beta_ridge = beta_ols /(1 + lambda), 
           beta_lasso = case_when(
               y > lambda ~ y - lambda, 
               y < -lambda ~ y + lambda, 
               .default = 0)) |>
    pivot_longer(starts_with("beta"), names_to="penalty", values_to="beta_hat") |>
    mutate(penalty = recode_values(
        penalty, 
        "beta_ols" ~ "OLS [No Penalty]", 
        "beta_ridge" ~ "Ridge Regression (Sum of Squares Penalty)", 
        "beta_lasso" ~ "LASSO Regression (Absolute Value Penalty)")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=y, y=beta_hat, color=penalty)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab(expression(y[i])) + 
    ylab("Estimated Coefficient\n(Different Penalties") + 
    theme(legend.position="bottom") + 
    scale_color_brewer(type="qual", 
                       palette=2, 
                       name="Penalty") + 
    ggtitle("Effect of Shrinkage Penalties", 
            expression(lambda==1))
```

Unsurpisingly, the OLS penalty is a straight-line and the ridge penalty is a
'flattened' version of that same line. (Why?) The LASSO effect is a 
bit more interesting. Near $0$, we see that it gives gives _more_ shrinkage 
than ridge and indeed zeros things out. Farther away (large values), we
see less shrinkage. So it seems that the LASSO indeed is giving us what we want: 
a bit more shrinkage, leading to actual selection (zeroing) of small values, 
near zero while putting a bit less of a thumb on thescale to shrink large 
values. 

Is this helpful? It depends what we believe about the world. If we believe that
there are a few strong effects and a lot of 'true zeros', this is clearly a 
reasonable modeling choice. But those situations are definitely not the norm: in
our wine example, do we expect that there are a few 'magic' words and _no other
words_ have _any_ ability to predict the final score? Not really...

In these situations, the benefits of sparsity are _interpretational_ and
_practical_: 

- What are the _most important_ words? These are hopefully the last ones that
  the LASSO will discard. 
- If we can only use a few features for engineering-type reasons (speed, cost
  of data collection, interpretability), which ones should we use? 

While we do have good rules of thumb for picking a good $\lambda$ (more to follow),
it is often just as useful to look at the _order_ that the Lasso picks and selects
features. 

```{r}
glmnet(X, y) |> 
    tidy() |> 
    group_by(term) |> 
    slice_max(lambda) |> 
    ungroup() |> 
    arrange(desc(abs(lambda))) |> 
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> 
    mutate(sign = sign(lambda)) |>
    select(term, final_lambda=lambda, sign) |>
    mutate(rank = dense_rank(final_lambda))
```

Here, I have pulled out each coefficient (each word) and found the largest
lambda at which it is still nonzero. After looking at the sign of its 
coefficient, I have ranked them by LASSO-implied usefulness (higher final
$\lambda$ implies the feature 'held on' longer implies more important). 
The results seem to be reasonable-again, with little knowledge of wine culture. 

So what is _actually_ important under this sort of lasso ranking? Well, 
predictive utility (clearly, as we are still basically doing ERM) is the 
baseline, but we can temper this a bit: 

- As always, predictive power is not necessarily 'true causal' effect 
  (kids shoes and IQ), but it is suggestive
- When we have _strongly_ correlated features, lasso will pick one more or less
  at random. (Think: left and right shoe sizes vs IQ in children. LASSO will be
  happy with just one (again, basically at random) since the difference between
  them is miniscule.) Contrast this to ridge which will 'split the difference'
  and include both at a smaller coefficient value. 
  
  The ridge behavior is a bit more robust here (if one feature 'goes weird' and
  takes an abnormal value, ridge will react about half as much as lasso might 
  since it averages them), but lasso clearly wins on parsimony.
- From the above, LASSO will do a bit better when there isn't much correlation
  among the features. This is theoretically quite nice - and useful in some 
  limited experimental settings - but under our 'many features occur when we 
  measure many related things' heuristic, the practical value of this is only
  so-so. 

Overall, LASSO and related methods are rarely the _last word_ in knowing what
"truly matters", but it provides us a quick, efficient, and easy-to-use 
framework that does about as well as any sparse method could do.
